Cell and systems biologyOctober 2026

Every line is a loop

A periodic table for biology

Kat TittertonMacrofluidics29 min readdraft for commentthe countcode

In short

Chemistry has a periodic table because electrons come in whole numbers. The circuits that run a cell have whole numbers too: how many feedback loops close, how many of them brake, and how many keep a running total. Count those and a table appears, with rows of 4, 9 and 16 elements and one entry that never closes. That entry is aging, and followed far enough it is a loop as well. Three real circuits, running live below, carry the argument: a switch, a clock and an adapter. Counted against 640 published models, the table comes out full in one band and nearly empty in the other, and the empty band is where to look next.

01the blank square

What Mendeleev could do that biology cannot

In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev did something that still looks like a magic trick. He laid the known elements out by weight, found that the pattern stuttered, and instead of forcing it he left holes. Then he described what would fill them: a metal a little heavier than aluminium, density near 6, with a particular oxide. Six years later gallium turned up in a zinc ore, density 5.9. The blank square had been a prediction.

Biology has never had a table that could do that. It has catalogues, pathways and parts lists longer than any one person can read, and no grid in which an empty cell says: something belongs here, and here is what it will do. The usual explanation is that life is too messy for whole numbers. This essay argues the reverse. Biology has whole numbers. They are just not in the sequence.

They are in the loops. The argument runs in five steps, and the rest of the page is those steps drawn out.

  1. A closed loop carries whole numbers; a sequence does not.
  2. A loop's sign fixes what it can do. Amplify and it can remember; brake and it can keep time; brake through a running total and it returns to its set point exactly.
  3. Count loops, brakes and running totals, and each row of the table has (n+1)² elements for n loops: 4, 9, 16. A census of 640 published models fills one band of it and leaves the other empty.
  4. Loops are models of the world's rhythms. The one thing with no rhythm, time itself, gets only a counter, and the counter is the element that never closes.
  5. Followed far enough, the counter is a loop one period longer, so the table is a helix that closes when life reproduces.

02integers

Biology's whole numbers are loops

Chemistry got its table because electrons fill shells in whole numbers; Mendeleev's grid is that counting rule made visible. Biology looks continuous almost everywhere you point a microscope, except in one place: topology. A closed loop carries whole numbers that an open line never does. Cut nothing, and the number of times the two strands of a closed DNA domain pass through each other is fixed. It splits into twist and writhe [1]:

Lk=Tw+Wr

Lk, linking number: how many times the two strands pass through each other. A whole number, fixed until a strand is cut.

Tw, twist: how the strands wind around the axis of the helix. Continuous.

Wr, writhe: how the axis coils over itself. Continuous, and traded against twist, which is why a plasmid can look twisted here and coiled there.

Mendeleev sorted by atomic weight and mostly got the order right, with a few inversions such as tellurium before iodine, until Moseley found atomic number underneath. Gene sequence is biology's atomic weight. Loop context is its atomic number. The inversions are real: at the EPHA4 locus, structural variants that leave every gene intact move a domain boundary, a cluster of limb enhancers lands on the wrong promoter, and a limb comes out malformed [2]. Same letters, different loop, different hand.

So take loops as the elements, ask what numbers they carry, and let the shape of the table follow. The first number is the sign.

03shape, pattern, function

Why the sign of a loop is its valence

Every circuit in a cell can be read three ways. Its shape is how the arrows close: how many loops there are, and whether each one amplifies or brakes. Its pattern is what the levels do in time once the circuit runs: settle, flip, tick, return. Its function is what the cell gets for its trouble: a memory, a clock, a sense of direction. The claim of this essay is that shape fixes pattern, and pattern is what the cell uses.

The first half of that claim is a theorem. René Thomas guessed it in 1981: holding more than one stable state needs an amplifying loop, and keeping a rhythm needs a braking one. Soulé proved the first rule in general in 2003 [3]; Snoussi and Gouzé proved the second in 1998, for braking loops of length two or more [4, 58, 59]. Tyson, Chen and Novák had already sorted the field's small circuits by what they do, sniffers, buzzers, toggles and blinkers, and matched each to a wiring diagram [31]. Before the proof, the play. Below is a ring of three repressors, the repressilator that Elowitz and Leibler built in E. coli in 2000 [37], with its arrows free to flip.

With one brake or three, it ticks. With none or two, it settles into one of two states: a switch. Signs multiply round a loop, so two brakes cancel like a double negative, and a loop brakes only when it holds an odd number of them. That is the whole idea behind the proof, in a figure.

what it saysTwo stable states need an amplifying loop. A sustained rhythm needs a braking loop.

the ideaBetween two stable states lies an unstable one, a hilltop, and a hilltop needs a push that feeds back on itself and grows. A rhythm needs something to push back, late.

what it does not sayThat the loop will do it. The rules are necessary, not sufficient: a brake with too little delay just settles, and an amplifier that is too weak just leans.

A third pattern comes from a brake with a particular kind of memory. If the brake acts not on the error but on the running total of the error, it keeps pushing until the total stops growing, which happens only when the error is zero. Control engineers call this integral feedback; it returns a system exactly to its set point under any steady load [5].

Three real circuits make the case, one per pattern. Each is drawn three ways below: as cell biology draws it, with the molecules moving at the rates the equations give them; as a loop of arrows; and as a signal on a strip chart. The sliders are the real parameters. Push them.

04the switch

A bacterium decides about lunch

Escherichia coli would rather eat glucose. When the glucose runs out and lactose is around, it has to decide whether to build the machinery to eat lactose: a pump to bring the sugar in and an enzyme to cut it. Building is expensive, so the cell should not build for a trace, and once it has built, it should not dither. A bacterium cannot afford to be a flip-flopper.

The lac operon settles the matter with a loop. Lactose inside the cell disables a repressor, LacI. LacI, when free, sits on the lacZYA genes and blocks them. One of those genes makes LacY, the pump that brings lactose in. Follow the arrows round: more pump, more lactose inside, less working LacI, more pump. Two repressions in one loop multiply like signs, (−)(−) = (+), and the loop amplifies.

On the way up nothing happens, and nothing happens, and then at about 0.9 the pump switches on and the sugar floods in. On the way down the pump stays on past 0.9, past 0.6, all the way down to about 0.3. Between those two levels the same cell can be on or off, depending on where it has been. That is memory, and it is what an amplifying loop is for [3]. Ozbudak and colleagues watched single E. coli do exactly this in 2004: at intermediate inducer, two populations in one tube, on and off, side by side [32]. Gardner, Cantor and Collins had built the same shape from two synthetic repressors four years earlier and got a switch out of it, as the shape says they must [33].

Shape: one loop, no brake. Pattern: two states, with a gap between the level that turns it on and the level that turns it off. Function: a decision that sticks. Every committee understands the value of the third thing and few achieve it.

05the clock

A thermostat with a long hallway

Nearly every cell in your body keeps time, and the mechanism is a brake. In the nucleus, two proteins, CLOCK and BMAL1, switch on the Per and Cry genes. The messenger RNAs leave the nucleus, PER and CRY proteins are made in the cytoplasm, pair up, travel back in, and sit on CLOCK and BMAL1 until the genes go quiet. Then PER and CRY are degraded, the brake lifts, and the genes come back on [34]. One loop, one bar.

A brake on its own does not tick. A thermostat settles. This one ticks because the brake arrives late: transcription takes time, so does translation, so does the trip back into the nucleus, so does the chemistry that lets PER and CRY act once they are there. By the time the brake lands, the genes have been on for hours and the cytoplasm is full of PER. By the time it lifts, the cell is empty of it. The delay is not a flaw in the clock. The delay is the clock [36].

At nine hours the loop ticks once a day. With no delay the ticking dies. The brake arrives before anything has built up, and the loop settles at a level, which is the theorem's small print made visible: a braking loop is necessary for a rhythm, not sufficient [4]. An element is a shape plus a regime, and the same shape at the wrong rates is a different element's neighbour.

The shape is older than the cell that carries it. Elowitz and Leibler wired three synthetic repressors into a ring in 2000, an odd number of bars, and the bacteria ticked [37]. Three cyanobacterial proteins, KaiA, KaiB and KaiC, keep a 24-hour beat in a test tube with ATP and nothing else [6]: a heavy isotope of the single braking loop, with the period written into the chemistry rather than the transcription.

Shape: one loop, one brake, late. Pattern: a wave. Function: a cell that is ready for dawn before dawn, which is the whole point of a clock, as opposed to a thermometer.

06the adapter

Steering with a memory a few seconds long

E. coli has no eyes and no ruler. It swims in straight runs, tumbles to pick a new direction, and steers up a gradient of food by one trick: if things are getting better, tumble less. The receptor that senses attractant drives the tumbling; attractant lowers the receptor's activity; so a cell swimming toward food keeps going. The problem is the next step. If attractant stayed high and activity stayed low, the cell would be blind to any further improvement. It has to return to the same tumbling rate at any background, and it has to do so exactly, or it would drift in one direction forever.

The trick is a count. One enzyme, CheR, adds methyl groups to the receptor at a steady rate. Another, CheB, removes them, and CheB is switched on by the receptor's own activity. So the number of methyl groups on the receptor is a running total of (set point − activity), and it keeps changing until activity is back at the set point, whatever the attractant outside [35]. Yi and colleagues showed in 2000 that this is integral feedback, the same arithmetic a cruise control uses to hold sixty on a hill [5].

After a step, activity dips, the methyl count climbs, and activity comes back to the line. With the leak, the count forgets as it adds, and activity settles above or below the set point by an amount that depends on the attractant. Without it, the return is exact, and the receptor can be as sensitive at the top of the gradient as at the bottom. Yeast do the same arithmetic with salt, over minutes rather than seconds [15].

Shape: one loop, one brake, acting through a running total. Pattern: a dip that returns to zero error. Function: a sense of direction built from comparing now with a few seconds ago.

Three shapes, three patterns, three jobs. The cell needed no new chemistry for any of them. It needed arrows closed in different ways. And a thing that can be counted can be put in a table.

07the table

Rows are loop count; period is mass

A periodic table needs whole-number axes; continuous quantities belong inside the cells. The whole numbers here are the number of independent loops in a circuit (ν), how many of them brake (k), and how many act through a running total (j). Period is continuous, so it goes in the cell, the way atomic mass does. That gives isotopes: an amplifying loop at milliseconds (a riboswitch) and at hours (the lac operon) are the same element at different rates, and KaiABC is a heavy isotope of the single brake; each element's card in Figure 6 lists its isotopes with their periods. The environment's real periods, the day, the month, the year, decide which isotopes are abundant, not where the cells sit; chemistry separates its table from nucleosynthesis the same way.

Row ν holds (ν+1)² elements, and the formula is just counting: each of the ν loops amplifies or brakes, so the number of brakes runs from 0 to ν, which is ν+1 choices; each loop also acts through a running total or not, another ν+1 choices; multiply. Element zero, the running total with no loop at all, is the one entry that never returns.

The + + + cell was blank in the first draft, and the blank was ignorance, not nature's. OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG each bind their own gene and each other's, a fully interconnected amplifying circuit [25]. The table says what such an element must do: amplifying feedback on a monotone system yields multiple stable states with hysteresis and cannot oscillate [26], so the occupant should be a memory with more than two settings and no clock. That is a stem cell's job description. The same reading fills the other two blanks in row 3.

the other two blanks of row 3

+ + −. Two amplifying loops can hold a state and one brake can end it. The receptor for epidermal growth factor, EGFR, is wired this way. It switches itself on; it and PTPRG, an enzyme that strips its activating tags, switch each other off; and a second such enzyme, PTPN2, closes a braking loop that sets how long the signal lasts [27]. The state it holds is a working memory: a cell keeps pointing toward where a growth signal was for about forty minutes after the signal is gone, and can still turn toward a new one [28].

− − −. With no amplifying loop there is only one state to be in [3], so three brakes can hold a level or keep a beat but cannot remember. NF-κB, the factor that turns on inflammation genes, makes its own three brakes, IκBα, IκBε and A20 [29, 30]. It pulses in and out of the nucleus, and after each pulse it needs 100 to 200 minutes before it can answer in full again [29].

If 4, 9 and 16 ring a bell, they are the numbers of orbitals in an atom's second, third and fourth shells, and the match runs deeper. Sort a row by l = max(k, j), the larger of its two counts, and it splits into layers of 1, 3, 5 and 7, the sizes of the s, p, d and f subshells; inside a layer, m = k − j runs from −l to l, as the magnetic number does. It is a counting identity, not physics, and it stops one step short: an atom's shells hold twice as many electrons because each orbital takes two, and that missing factor of two reads as a missing binary, perhaps the order in which loops nest. Chapter 13 puts that guess to the test.

(n+1)2=∑l=0n(2l+1)

Others had sorted circuits by their loops before: oscillators [36], the named small circuits [31], the wiring patterns that recur across organisms [43, 44]. The table puts the three counts together, much as Ahnert and colleagues built a periodic table for protein complexes [45]. Here it is, every element named, with what the next chapter's census found already marked. Tap an element to read it:

The blanks are the point. A table earns the name by its gaps, and this one has two kinds: cells that should fill with search, and a single entry the closure logic cannot reach. If it is a real periodic table, three things should be true. Circuits with a given number of loops do no more kinds of things than their row has elements. No circuit does what its loops forbid: no switch without an amplifying loop, no clock without a brake. And every element can be built, so each blank is a prediction. The second is the theorem of chapter 03; the other two are open. To test them, count real circuits.

08the count

Count the circuits that exist

A table that predicts can be checked against a catalogue. BioModels is a public library of the mathematical models behind published papers, founded in 2005 [41], each model checked against its paper and stored in a standard format [40, 42]: the cell cycle, the fruit fly's day clock, calcium spikes and more. The census took the 640 models of the 2017 release, the one Baudier, Fages and Soliman had already mined for Thomas's positive-loop condition, so the counts can be compared [24]. It drew each model's arrows, listed its loops, dropped the ones chemistry makes for free (Supplement B), and placed each circuit on the table.

Of the 613 models the census could read, 175 have one to three loops, few enough to place. They fall in one band. Every element without a running total is filled, all 10 of them, and familiar circuits sit where their biology puts them: the repressilator under one brake, the trp operon under two. Of the 20 elements with a running total, 3 are filled, by 4 models between them. The table is fullest where biology already had words for what it saw, switches and clocks, and emptiest where the words arrived last.

The three claims are scored below. The second is a theorem, so it checks the code rather than the biology; the first holds softly, since each model ran at one setting of its rates; the third is where the weakness is: no reading of the equations finds a running total cleanly, not even in yeast, where experiments pinned one down [15].

The last row is the surprise. The fruit fly's day clock has five curated models, all built from the same proteins, and they land in four places. Measure a coastline with a shorter ruler and it gets longer; a loop count grows the same way as a model gains detail (Supplement C). Proton number does not depend on how you draw an atom; loop number depends on how you draw a circuit, and a count on a reduced model, with the fast binding steps merged, is the first thing to fix.

So the table has a full band and an empty one. Chemistry's table had empty squares too, and what those turned out to hold, and why they were empty for so long, is the best guide to these.

09the hidden elements

What the empty band would do in a cell

The empty band is the running-total column: twenty elements, seventeen of them blank. Each has a parent in the full band, and each should behave like its parent with one thing added, because a running total does one of two things depending on the loop it sits on. On a braking loop it makes the loop return to its set point exactly, as chemotaxis does; that is a theorem [5, 46]. On an amplifying loop it should add up its input and commit once the total is high enough; that is a hypothesis, and it is this essay's eka-aluminium. Reading each blank from its parent, the way Mendeleev read gallium from aluminium, gives the table's predictions (every one is in its card in Figure 6). The one worth building first is the table's gallium.

Sw∫, a switch with a running total (element 2). Flips on how long a signal has lasted rather than how strong it is: a dose timer, a switch that commits after exposure. Look for it where a cell must decide whether a signal is real, at commitment points in the cell cycle and in cell fate. Nothing in the census sits there yet. It does not exist in any published model, but it can be built from parts this page already has: take the lac switch of Figure 2 and feed it the running total of a pulse instead of lactose.

three more of the table's predictions
  • Ad, the adapter (element 3). A brake through a running total: responds to a change, then returns exactly to where it was. Known from experiments in chemotaxis and osmotic stress [5, 15, 35], built as a synthetic part in bacteria [47], and found by the census in no model at all: the first clue that the band is hidden rather than empty.
  • Me∫, a memory with a running total (element 6). A memory that counts: holds one of several states and moves to the next once enough has accumulated. Look for it in cells that count pulses or divisions before changing state.
  • Ro∫, Ro∫² and Ci∫ (elements 7, 10 and 21). A relaxation oscillator, and the day clock, with a running total inside: a beat whose baseline is held exactly while it fires. These three the census did find, four models between them, so the band is not empty everywhere.

Why would seventeen elements be missing? Chemistry's table had the same problem, and its elements went missing for four different reasons, each with its own cure. The first is the one the synthetic biologists have already repeated.

It decays before you can weigh it. Technetium, element 43, has no stable isotope, so none survived in the Earth's crust to be dug up; it was made in a cyclotron in 1937, before it was ever found in nature [48]. Promethium, 61, was identified in fission products ten years later [62]. The loop table's version: an exact running total needs special chemistry, such as two molecules that destroy each other [46], and the first one was built in bacteria in 2019 [47, 52] before anyone found one in a published model. Made before found.

three more reasons, each with its cure
  • It does nothing the method can see. Argon and the other noble gases do not react, so chemistry had no handle on them; Rayleigh and Ramsay found argon in 1895 from a discrepancy, nitrogen from air weighing more than nitrogen from compounds [60]. The loop table's version: a running total shows itself only under a sustained step, as an exact return where a plain brake would sag, and a census that reads static equations has no handle on it. The cure is dynamic: drive the model, watch the return.
  • It hides among look-alikes. Hafnium sat in zirconium ores, chemically a twin, until Bohr said where to look and Coster and Hevesy found it by its X-ray spectrum in 1923 [61], the spectra by which Moseley had just ordered the elements by number rather than weight [39]. The loop table's version: a loop through a running total draws the same picture as a plain braking loop. Only its response to a frequency sweep tells them apart, which is why the assay in chapter 13 needs a pump and a camera rather than a parts list.
  • It is simply not found yet. Gallium, scandium and germanium filled Mendeleev's squares within fifteen years, and some of his other predictions never came true at all [38]. The census read a 2017 release; running totals entered the field's vocabulary in 2000 [5] and were built as parts by 2019 [47]. Newer releases, and computer-built circuits searched for exact adaptation [50], may fill the band.

What does the empty band say about the hypothesis? That the table is two thirds proven and one third promised. Loops and brakes are real axes: circuits spread across every combination of them. Running totals are, so far, an axis with almost no one on it. If the band stays empty after dynamic readings and newer releases, the honest move is Mendeleev's: retire the axis, and each row shrinks from (ν+1)² elements to ν+1, which is 2, 3 and 4. If the band fills, the square count stands. Either outcome is a result. Which raises the question the table cannot answer by itself: why would nature count loops at all?

10loops are models

Why a cell carries a copy of its world

Because loops hold information, and they hold it because loops are models. Conant and Ashby proved in 1970 that a regulator which is maximally successful and simple must be isomorphic to the system it regulates [7]. Francis and Wonham made the linear case rigorous in 1976: a controller that robustly cancels a class of disturbances contains a copy of their generator, the simplest machine that could have produced them [8]. Sontag extended the result to adaptation with signal detection, and named circadian clocks as candidate internal models of the day [9]. Integral feedback is the model of a constant input, which is why chemotaxis adapts exactly [5]. An entrained oscillator is a copy of the planet's rotation. The clock in chapter 05 is not a reaction to the day. It is a portrait of it.

This derives the table instead of sorting into it. Rows are periods because the environment's spectrum is discrete: molecular, tidal, daily, lunar, annual, generational. Columns are the generators a loop can copy: a constant, a pair of states, a sinusoid. Nesting is nested models, a day inside a year.

The open column follows from the same principle, with one detail worth stating exactly. Sontag's theorem assumes the generating system is Poisson-stable, meaning its trajectories keep returning near where they began [9]. Every periodic signal qualifies. A monotonic signal does not, and its only generators are integrators, which fill without bound. A bounded cell can carry a bounded copy of every recurrent feature of its world, while its copy of time can only be a counter that never resets. Read this way, the epigenetic clock is not damage. It is the internal model of time's arrow, with the one property such a model must have: it does not come back.

Unless you follow it far enough.

11the table is a loop

The true shape of a periodic table

Mendeleev's grid is a cut. Seven years before him, de Chancourtois wound the elements by weight along a helix on a cylinder, one turn per period, and the elements that behave alike fell on vertical lines [10]. The periodic law is itself a loop: go up in atomic number and the properties come back around. A grid hides that. A spiral shows it, and the figure at the top of this page winds both tables into theirs: one turn per row, memories on one ray and clocks on the other, element zero at the centre with nothing to wind. That is the punchline of the title, and it reaches one entry further.

The same geometry runs on into the table's one open entry. A line is a loop you have not followed far enough. Every isotope of element zero (its card in Figure 6 lists them) is a loop seen from inside its own period: differentiation is an arc of development, aging an arc of the germline. Line those isotopes up by period and each hands off to a closed loop one period longer, which strings the periods into the helix de Chancourtois drew.

The helix bites its tail once. Reproduction rejoins the last row to the first, and the reset is measurable: epigenetic age falls to a minimum around gastrulation, the ground zero from which aging is then counted [11]. Partial reprogramming with OSK restores youthful methylation and vision in old mice [12], a chord drawn across the same circle. The germline is the loop and the soma is the arc that does not come back, which is Kirkwood's disposable soma restated as topology [13].

One closure is missing. Lineages never reset, because no generator exists for the gene pool, so evolution stays a line threaded through the hole of the torus. Individuals loop; lineages do not. Biology closes the arrow of time for organisms only, which may be why aging feels programmed from inside and random from above.

12three diseases

One algebra for cancer, autoimmunity and neurodegeneration

In loop language a disease is a loop whose model no longer matches the world, or a loop that has opened. Three of the big ones are the same failure in three tissues: an amplifying loop held on while its brake is deleted, so a process that should close runs as a counter.

Cancer. Tissue growth is a switch held by brakes: tumour suppressors, contact inhibition, apoptosis, senescence. Two of the hallmarks of cancer are exactly the switch held on and the brakes deleted, sustaining proliferative signalling and evading growth suppressors [17]. The decisive experiment exists. Restoring p53, one brake, in established mouse tumours caused regression, by apoptosis in lymphomas and by senescence in sarcomas and liver carcinomas [18, 19]. Close the loop and the counter stops.

the same loop in autoimmunity and neurodegeneration

Autoimmunity. Immune memory is a switch; regulatory T cells and checkpoints are its brakes. Delete the brake genetically and you get IPEX, where FOXP3 mutations remove regulatory T cells and cause fatal multi-organ autoimmunity [20]. Delete it on purpose and you get the same thing under a different name: checkpoint blockade treats cancer by removing the brakes on T cells, and its immune-related adverse events are autoimmunity in the same patient [21]. Cancer and autoimmunity are one loop with the sign of the intervention flipped.

Neurodegeneration. Seeded aggregation is an amplifying loop: a misfolded seed converts healthy protein into more seeds [22]. Clearance is the brake that should close it. Dividing cells also have a reset: yeast mother cells keep the damaged proteins and daughters are born clean [23]. Neurons never divide, so they have no reset and no dilution by growth; when clearance fails, the aggregation switch runs as a counter for the organism's whole life. That is why these are diseases of late life: their clock is the aging counter itself.

None of this is new biology. What the table adds is a prediction across all three: the lost brake should show up as a missing resonance in a frequency sweep before pathology does, and the same two interventions, close the brake or impose a reset, should work in each.

13what comes next

Science is a loop too

The census closes one turn of a loop that runs through this whole page: an idea, a prediction, a test, a result, a refined idea. It cannot falsify the count itself, any more than a die can roll a seven, but it says what the next turn should carry.

Here is one turn of it, run on this page. Chapter 07 ended on a guess: the table is a factor of two short of chemistry, and the missing binary might be the order in which loops nest, which loop is the faster, inner one. A guess is a prediction, so it can be tested, and this one can be tested three ways: by counting, with a toy, and on the census.

The count says no. Chemistry's factor of two is spin, and spin doubles every shell, the first one included. Nesting order needs two loops to compare, so it cannot touch the rows with none or one, and ordering every loop from fast to slow gives 4, 16 and 64 arrangements where doubling needs 8, 18 and 32. Whatever the missing binary is, it is not this.

The toy says the guess was not empty either. Take one amplifying loop and one brake through the same gene, draw the rates at random 800 times, and run every draw twice: once with the amplifier fast and the brake slow, once the other way round. All 32 draws that keep time do it with the amplifier fast. Swap the speeds and every one of them stops. This is the relaxation oscillator of the textbooks [36]: a fast switch flips, a slow brake drags it back, and the beat is the round trip. Order adds no new element. It chooses which of an element's behaviours appears, which makes it part of the regime, like the rates, rather than a new count.

The census leans the same way without settling it. Timed in the models' own equations, by how long a signal takes to cross the molecules each loop does not share with the other, 11 of the 16 real two-loop circuits whose amplifier is faster keep time, against 4 of the 9 whose brake is faster. With so few models, a gap that size turns up by chance about one time in five. Timing the loops by the strength of their arrows instead shows no gap at all, so the way speed is measured matters as much as the circuit.

So the turn ends the way good turns end. The guess is retired, a rule survives it, fast amplifier and slow brake make a clock, and the original question is still open: the table is a factor of two short of chemistry, and the next guess has to touch every row, element zero included.

Chemistry's table went on to predict materials and medicines: eka-silicon became germanium and then the first transistor [49], and element 43 was made before it was found [48]. For cells, the same three gifts. For the field, a shared address: a model says which element it is, a reader asks whether its behaviour matches, and circuits built from different molecules in different organisms can turn out to be the same element, as the fly's clock and ours are at their coarsest drawing, one braking loop through transcription. For medicine, a diagnosis by element, which loop to put back rather than which molecule to hit, with p53 restoration and checkpoint blockade as the first two cases (chapter 12). For technology, design by position, as a chemist who needs a reactive metal looks in the first column: a sensor that must reset exactly comes from Ad, where the circuit built in bacteria is the first part in the box [47, 52], and a timer that commits after a dose comes from Sw∫, which nobody has built in a cell. Figure 8 is the recipe: wire a toggle switch to a running total and drive it with pulses of different lengths; if it flips on the total rather than the peak, Sw∫ is made before it is found. And the first test of the count itself is every small circuit built on a computer and run across its rates [50, 51].

An automated lab could run most of this. It needs three things a molecular parts list does not give it: a finite hypothesis space, an assay it can run without hand-built reagents, and rules for throwing models away before fitting them. The table supplies all three, and a few things besides.

the six things an automated lab gets
  1. A hypothesis space it can enumerate. A cell's loop content is a point in (ν, k, j) plus a regime, a few hundred cases at most, instead of an open-ended network of molecules.
  2. An assay with no parts list. A frequency sweep: periodic input, label-free time series, fit the transfer function, read off the generators. It needs a pump and a camera, not an antibody, so an agent can run it closed-loop and overnight.
  3. Rejection rules. Thomas's conditions, the nesting rule that no clock runs faster than its sub-loops, and the (ν+1)² bound all discard candidate models before a single parameter is fit.
  4. Borrowed tools. Loop content is system identification, so sixty years of control-theory code applies unchanged.
  5. A different objective. The intervention search runs over loop-closing moves, restore a brake, entrain a clock, impose a reset, rather than over parts to inhibit.
  6. A provenance ledger. Every claim here is tagged theorem, derivation or pattern, which is the weighting an agent needs to decide what to trust.

Six experiments would settle the rest, each with the outcome that would kill it. The first has been run: it is chapter 08.

the six experiments
  1. Count the elements. Curate the two- and three-loop circuits in a model database, classify each by what it does, and count the kinds; mining BioModels for circuit structure has been done for Thomas's positive-loop condition [24]. Prediction: 9 and 16. More kills the rule; fewer names the quantum number that is dead weight.
  2. Sweep a cell. Drive cells with periodic osmotic or nutrient input in a microfluidic device, record a label-free time series, fit the frequency response, as was done for the yeast osmo-adaptation pathway [14, 15]. Prediction: the fitted generators land in the table's cells, and the rows are discrete. Resonances that fall between cells, with no circuit behind them, kill the integer axis.
  3. Hunt the forbidden element. Search the same databases for a multi-loop oscillator faster than its own sub-loops. One verified instance kills the nesting rule.
  4. Dig for a niche fossil. Compare the frequency response of lineages evolved for thousands of generations in constant conditions with their ancestors. Prediction: one specific resonance gone, the loop that modelled the feature held constant. General decay with no specific loss kills the model-of-the-world reading.
  5. Watch the reset. Track epigenetic age at single-cell resolution through gastrulation and through partial reprogramming. Prediction: a counter emptied, a monotone fall to a floor, rather than a loop restored, which would oscillate or overshoot.
  6. Find the loop before the disease. In models of each disease in Figure 11, sweep before pathology appears. Prediction: the brake is already missing from the response. Then close it, as p53 restoration did [18, 19], and the counter should stop. A disease whose sweep looks normal until the end kills the mismatch reading for that disease.

14what it does not do

How much of this is proved

The claims above are not equally secure. Four are theorems, three are derivations or definitions, and the rest are patterns and restatements of other people's results; the ledger below grades each one. The census adds limits of its own. Behaviour was read at published parameters from twelve starts, so it undercounts kinds of behaviour. The loop filters are proved for amplifying loops only, and applied to braking loops they remove the brakes of 10 clocks. Loops written as formulas rather than reactions are invisible to it (13 models), and 102 loop searches stopped at their step limit. And BioModels holds what people chose to model and publish, not a random sample of biology.

the provenance ledger
ClaimStatusRests on

The missing factor of two is nesting ordertested, rejectedOrder cannot touch rows with fewer than two loops and ordering gives 4, 16, 64, not 8, 18, 32; it does decide whether a mixed circuit keeps time (toy, all 32 clocks), and the census leans the same way, 11 of 16 against 4 of 9, not significant[36], chapter 13

What each hidden element would dopredictionRead from each blank's parent; the adapting half rests on a theorem, the accumulating half is a hypothesis[5, 46]
The + + + cell is a multistate memory with no clock (pluripotency core)predictionFrom monotone-systems theory; the occupant is established, the count is not[25, 26]
The + + − cell holds EGFR's working memory; the − − − cell holds NF-κB's pulsespatternEach source names the three loops, which meet at a single node, so the count does not depend on how the loops are chosen; wider module boundaries add loops[27–30]
Cancer, autoimmunity and neurodegeneration as a lost brakerestatementOf established results; the cross-disease prediction is untested[17–23]

Three holes are visible from here. Space is missing: a Turing pattern is a clock with a wavelength, and the segmentation clock converts time into space, so the real table has period and wavelength as its rows. Mechanism is missing by design: the table says which generators a cell carries, never which molecules carry them, as Mendeleev's grid said nothing about bonds. And the counting rule, the one thing that would turn this from a lens into a foundation, is derived here and tested only once, by the census of chapter 08, which found one band of the table full and the other nearly empty. The factor of two the table is short of chemistry is still unexplained: nesting order, the first guess, failed its test in chapter 13.

The examples in the element cards of Figure 6 are approximate, drawn from textbooks, and invite correction. The three models in Figures 2 to 4 are caricatures built to show a shape, with their equations and checks in the repository, and they invite replacement by the real ones.

Mendeleev's blank square held a prediction because he had found the right thing to count. The claim here is that biology's right thing is a loop, that a cell deciding about lunch, keeping time and steering toward food are the first three entries, and that the table they sit in is a loop as well. Its gallium is still out there: a switch that keeps a running total, somewhere a cell has to decide how long a signal has lasted. Every line is a loop. Follow yours.

15supplement

The census in depth

Four supplements hold the rest of the evidence, with every figure, setting and equation. All of it is open: the code, the data and these supplements live in one repository, and one command rebuilds every number on this page from the raw download in about two hours on a laptop. Change a definition, rerun, and see where your favourite circuit lands.

A. The elements as tiles
B. How the census works and how it was checked

Chemistry makes loops that regulate nothing. Binding and unbinding go out and back, like a two-way street, not round, like a roundabout. The filters of Baudier, Fages and Soliman [24], built on Soliman’s condition [54], remove them. They proved that dropping these loops loses no amplifying loop that could hold two states; the proof covers amplifying loops only (Supplement D).

Validation. Toy models with known answers are counted on every build, and Tyson, Chen and Novák’s seven textbook circuits [31] serve as an answer key. On the same release, Baudier, Fages and Soliman found no braking loop in 14% of models; this census finds none in 13%. An audit of the first full run found a backtracking bug that cost 42 of 106 rate-rule models some loops, and after the fix the small-model count fell from 179 to 175. Two independent runs from the raw download produce identical files.

C. More results: loop counts, behaviour, detail

Sorted by six behaviours and their mixtures, one loop gives 6 kinds, two loops 9 and three loops 6; merged into four behaviours, 4, 5 and 4. Neither two nor three loops shows more kinds of behaviour than it has elements, so by the essay’s own terms the rule survives. One loop shows more than its 4, though the essay set its test at two and three loops, and merged into four behaviours it gives exactly 4. The fruit fly’s clock models: Goldbeter’s 1995 model has one loop (−); Tyson and colleagues’ 1999 model has two (+ −); Leloup and Goldbeter’s 1998 and 1999 models have two each (− −); and their 1999 model with Gonze has 14. The paired running-total reading finds six models with a total kept by two molecules; one, a folate pathway, has it on a loop.

D. Methods: every step, setting and equation

Every step is a script in the analysis folder beside this page, and every setting that can move a number is given here. The data flow top to bottom:

Models into equations

BioModels release 31 (26 June 2017) holds 640 curated models, the set Baudier, Fages and Soliman used [24]. Each is read with libSBML [56], with function definitions expanded, and compiled by libRoadRunner [55]. The variables x are the species that change and are not fixed by an assignment rule, plus any quantity with a rate rule. With v(x) the reaction rates and N the stoichiometry matrix, whose entry Nkj is how many of molecule k reaction j makes (positive) or uses up (negative), each model is

dxdt=Nv(x)

plus the right-hand sides of its rate rules. 613 models could be read this way. Of the other 27, 5 use delay equations, 3 use logical rules, 6 have values roadrunner cannot set and 13 gave no arrows at the states read, among them Tyson’s mutual-inhibition switch, whose loop is hidden inside a formula.

Arrows

An arrow runs from molecule i to molecule k through reaction j when reaction j changes k and its rate depends on i. Its sign multiplies two signs: whether the rate rises or falls with i, and whether the reaction makes or uses up k.

σik(j)=sgn(∂vj∂xi)·sgn(Nkj)

The derivative is a central difference, with step h equal to a tenth of a percent of xi:

∂vj∂xi≈vj(x+hei)−vj(x−hei)2h

A difference smaller than 10−13 of the two rates counts as zero. Signs are read at five states of the model’s own run, t = 0, 1, 10, 100 and 1000, each reached from a fresh reset, so events and the clock apply only where they belong and one failed run loses one state, not all. A species sitting at exactly zero is lifted to 10−6 of the median level so its arrows can be read. An arrow seen at any of the five states counts, so one arrow can carry both signs. Rate rules give arrows the same way, from the derivative of their right-hand side.

Self-loops need care, because every molecule that decays has a trivial braking loop on itself. Decay, consumption and reverse flux are not counted. A braking self-loop is kept only when a reaction that makes the molecule slows as it rises, and its rate law stays non-negative when the molecule is pushed a thousand times higher (end-product inhibition, autorepression); a symbolic test with sympy looks for a positive root of the rate law’s numerator. An amplifying self-loop is dropped when it only comes from a substrate written as a total minus the molecule itself.

As a check, signs were also read at random states, each variable drawn log-uniformly between the lowest and highest levels it reaches on its own run to t = 1000. It gives 4 of 9 elements at two loops and 5 of 16 at three, and the two proven rules still hold.

Loops

A loop is an elementary circuit of the arrow graph, with each arc labelled by its reaction. Its sign is the product of its arcs’ signs, so it brakes when it holds an odd number of brakes:

sign(L)=∏a∈Lσa

Baudier, Fages and Soliman proved that three kinds of loop can be dropped without losing any amplifying loop that could hold two states [24]. The proofs run through the Jacobian; in plain terms, with the intuition for each:

  • A loop that uses two arrows from the same reaction, or from reactions that are the same up to a positive factor (stoichiometry columns that are positive multiples of each other). One reaction cannot amplify itself.
  • A loop that uses a reaction and its reverse (columns that are negative multiples). Out and back is not a loop.
  • A loop whose molecules make up a whole conserved pool, a weighting p ≥ 0 with pTN = 0 that no reaction changes. Moving material round a closed pool pushes nothing.

The proofs cover amplifying loops only. There is no matching theorem for braking loops, so applying the filters to them is a choice, and the alternative split below counts braking loops as drawn. A fourth test, the rank condition from the same paper, keeps a loop only if its reactions are independent, so that their stoichiometry columns cannot be combined to cancel; it drops cycles that just move material round:

rankN[:,R(L)]=|L|

Loops are listed by depth-first search from each molecule s through higher-numbered molecules in s’s strongly connected component, refusing an arc the moment it would break a filter. A search stops after 5,000,000 steps or 20,000 loops, and the model then counts as “search unfinished”. Counting steps instead of seconds is what makes reruns identical. Whether any amplifying loop survives the filters is decided separately by their vertex-elimination algorithm, which finishes even when listing doesn’t.

Each model gets three counts: c loops, k of them braking, j of them through a running total. The essay counts independent loops instead, the cyclomatic number of the union of all loops,

ν=E−V+C

with E arrows, V molecules and C connected pieces. It differs from c in 1 of the 175 small models. Sontag’s distance to positive feedback [53], the fewest sign flips that make every loop amplifying, gives a braking count that doesn’t depend on which loops are listed. Computed on the filtered loops, it differs from k in 17 of the 175.

Loops countedonetwothree
every loop, as drawn403437
after the filters676745
after the filters and the rank test (used here)676543

Running totals

Strict reading. Molecule i keeps a running total if its own name appears in none of the rate laws that change it, so its rate cannot depend on its level:

∂fi∂xi≡0

Loose reading. Molecule i nearly keeps one if its own level moves its net rate by less than a tenth of the flow into it, at the last state reached (first-order decay scores exactly 1 at steady state):

ri=|∂fi/∂xi||xi|Φi<0.1 Φi=∑jmax(Nijvj,0)

Paired reading. Two molecules a and b keep one together if a weighted sum z of them changes at a rate that depends on neither, nor on any molecule P that shares a conserved total with them, but does depend on something else:

z=caxa+cbxb,∂z˙∂xq=0forq∈S∪P

A paired running total is two molecules whose weighted sum changes at a rate that depends on neither of them. The code screens for candidates numerically, then confirms each one exactly from the rate laws. Candidates come from the Jacobian J = N ∂v/∂x at the five states. The block J[S, S ∪ P] for S = {a, b}, stacked across states, must have rank one (smallest singular value under 10−4 of the largest, rows normalised). Sums equal to one molecule plus a constant once conserved totals are used are dropped. Each survivor is then confirmed from the rate laws: the weights are rounded to a ratio of whole numbers up to 12, sympy differentiates the weighted rate exactly, and the derivative must cancel to 10−9 at four random states spread over six orders of magnitude, with parameters at the model’s values. 31 candidates whose rate laws use conditional formulas could not be confirmed and are left out.

The readings were checked on models where the answer is known:

ModelLoopsStrictLoose
yeast osmoregulation, has one (Schaber 2012)113noneglycerol outside the cell and the glycerol-making protein
yeast osmoadaptation, has one (Petelenz-Kurdziel 2013)2,026noneacetate, ethanol and glycerol outside the cell; biomass
cell cycle, two variables, has one (Tyson 1991)2total cyclintotal cyclin
feed-forward adapter, no loop, has none (Tyson 2003)0nonenone
chemotaxis, receptor complex only, has none (Bray 1995)thousandsnonenone
chemotaxis, phosphorylation steps only, has none (Bray 1993)thousandsnonetwo receptor complexes

The paired reading finds none in these six, finds the controller’s total in the toy, and finds nothing in the enzyme or the ring.

Behaviour

Each model runs at its published rates from its own start and eleven others. The others keep every conserved total of the start: they are corners of the set of states x ≥ 0 reachable as x0 + Nξ and capped at ten times the largest starting level, found by linear programs with random objectives, then mixed with Dirichlet(0.3) weights. The solver is CVODE [57] with relative tolerance 10−8 and absolute tolerance 10−12. Each run tries horizons of 102, 103, 104 and 105 time units, 2,001 samples each, and stops at the first that decides:

LabelRule
settlesover the last fifth of the run every variable moves by less than 10−5 of its level
rings, then settlessettles after crossing its final value at least twice, by more than 10−3 of it
keeps timein the second half, at least three peaks, a relative swing above 10−3, the last peak at least 0.9 of the first, and still at least 0.8 of that swing over a further 2T
holds two statesruns settle in two or more states more than 1% apart, but no more than a third as many states as runs, and no state has a zero eigenvalue in the Jacobian restricted to its conserved totals
settles anywhereend states that differ but have a zero eigenvalue, or are too many to be a few separate states: a line of resting states
grows without limita variable passes 106 times its starting scale, or is still climbing at the last horizon
driven from outsidethe model has events, or time appears in a rate law, rule or function; set aside (178 models)

432 models run on their own; 11 small models never settle under these rules. Finding two states from twelve starts at one setting of the rates is a lower bound.

The proven rules

Two of the table’s rules are theorems, so the census uses them to check itself.

Two states need an amplifying loop. Soulé proved it [3]: if a system of smooth rate equations has two separate steady states, then at some state in between, the arrows the census draws (the signed Jacobian) contain an amplifying loop. The idea, roughly: between two stable states lies an unstable one, a hilltop, and a hilltop needs a disturbance that feeds back on itself and grows, which is an amplifying loop. Baudier, Fages and Soliman sharpened the statement for reaction networks: the loop can be taken to be one that survives their filters [24]. The census checks this with their elimination algorithm, which decides whether such a loop exists without listing loops.

A sustained rhythm needs a braking loop. Snoussi and Gouzé proved that a stable oscillation needs a braking loop through at least two molecules [58, 59]. The idea: to swing, a system must overshoot and turn back, and turning back means some chain of arrows eventually pushes the other way, which multiplies to a brake. The census checks it exactly: a strongly connected piece of the graph has no braking loop just when its molecules split into two camps so that every arrow’s sign is the product of its ends’ camps,

σab=sasb,sa∈{+1,−1}

which a single pass of two-colouring decides. Braking self-loops are left out of this check, as the theorem requires.

What the theorems do not say: they are necessary conditions, not sufficient ones. An amplifying loop does not guarantee two states, and a braking loop does not guarantee a rhythm. They also speak of the signs at some state of the system, which is why the census reads signs where each model actually runs, and again at random states as a check.

Counting elements

A model with c = ν loops goes in element (ν, k, j), and row ν has (ν + 1)2 elements. Grouping them like orbitals gives each one an address, with layers of 2l + 1:

n=ν+1,l=max(k,j),m=k−j (ν+1)2=∑l=0ν(2l+1)

Two other counts treat each loop as carrying its own type. If every loop is one of four types (amplifying or braking, with or without a running total), a row is a multiset of ν types: 4, 10 and 20 elements, of which the models fill 5 at two loops and 5 at three. If only braking loops can keep a running total, three types give 3, 6 and 10 elements, of which they fill 4 and 5. Counting amplifying loops after the filters and braking loops as drawn, the split the proofs support, moves 85 models to another cell; every sign pattern stays filled, and no clock is left without a brake. Kinds of behaviour are the distinct sets of labels among the models of a row that run on their own.

Replication

Baudier, Fages and Soliman ran the same three filters on the same release:

Baudier, Fages and Soliman, Table 1: 506 modelsThis census: 540 models with reactions
No braking loop14%13%
No amplifying loop9%5%
No amplifying loop after the filters21%15%

Amplifying loops differ in a direction sign reading can’t explain, because reading every setting at once, as they did, can only add arrows. The gap more likely comes from how each pipeline turns a model file into reactions; theirs rebuilds some models from their equations. Their headline, 160 of 506, adds a rewiring test not run here. Their case study, the ERK cascade of model 270, comes out as they found it: 18 loops survive the filters, all braking, so it cannot hold two states.

Reproducing it

SettingValue
DataBioModels release 31, 193 MB, SHA-256 b6fba03e…0532, checked on download
SoftwarePython 3.9.6, libRoadRunner 2.7.0, python-libsbml 5.20.4, numpy 1.26.4, scipy 1.13.1, sympy 1.14.0 (all pinned in requirements.txt)
Randomnessevery draw seeded; parallel jobs write results in model order
Loop search5,000,000 steps or 20,000 loops per model; elimination capped at 300,000 arcs
Time limits1,200 s per model for loops, 900 s for behaviour, 240 s for running totals
Threadsone per job (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1), so parallel jobs don’t fight over the CPU
Run timeabout two hours with 8 jobs on a 10-core laptop

Two full runs from the raw download, in separate folders, gave identical files apart from the recorded timings. build_post.py writes this page from the results and refuses to build if a sentence no longer matches the data.
